extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proofs and elementary number theory (intro to proofs)
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook material teaching methods for constructing and evaluating mathematical proofs: definitions and proofs about perfect numbers (Euclid/Euler), methods for disproving statements (counterexamples, contradiction), and techniques of mathematical induction including strong induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a perfect number
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural number p is perfect if the sum of its positive divisors that are less than p equals p. (Equivalent formulation used later: p is perfect iff the sum of all its positive divisors equals 2p.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 6 = 1+2+3, 28 = 1+2+4+7+14, 496, 8128. The alternative definition (sum of all divisors = 2p) is simpler because it avoids special-casing p itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form (Euclid) that produces perfect numbers (set A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define A = {2^{n-1}(2^n - 1) : n ∈ N and 2^n - 1 is prime}. Every element of A is perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the form to generate concrete examples (n=2,3,5,7,13 give 6,28,496,8128,33550336). Primes of the form 2^n - 1 are Mersenne primes; when 2^n-1 is prime, 2^{n-1}(2^n - 1) is a perfect number (Euclid's theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use geometric series to sum divisors in proofs about perfect numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the formula ∑_{k=0}^{n-1} 2^k = 2^n - 1 to compute sums of powers of two appearing among divisors of numbers of the form 2^{n-1}(2^n-1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerate the divisors that are powers of two (and the corresponding multiples by the Mersenne prime) and use the geometric-series identity to show the sum of proper divisors equals the number (or equivalently that the sum of all divisors equals 2p). Equation references and worked algebra are provided in the Euclid-style proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving set inclusion / equality by proving both directions
rubrics_metrics.description: To show A = E (or A = P), prove A ⊆ E and E ⊆ A separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to show A = set of even perfect numbers E, first show every element of A is an even perfect number (A ⊆ E), then take an arbitrary even perfect p ∈ E, factor p and show it must have the Euclid form p = 2^{n-1}(2^n - 1) with 2^n - 1 prime (E ⊆ A). Classic two-direction strategy for set equality is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove membership by assuming generic element and deriving defining property
rubrics_metrics.description: To show an element belongs to a target set (e.g., A ⊆ P), assume p ∈ A and show p satisfies the defining property of P (e.g., p is perfect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked example: assume p = 2^{n-1}(2^n -1) with 2^n -1 prime, list all positive divisors of p, sum them (using geometric series) excluding p to verify sum equals p.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to disprove a statement (general principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove a statement P, prove its negation ¬P. (Stated succinctly: How to disprove P: Prove ¬P.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of ¬P can be done by direct methods, contrapositive, or contradiction. The text emphasizes this as the foundational idea for disproofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproving universally quantified statements: counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove a universally quantified statement ∀x ∈ S, P(x), produce an example x ∈ S for which P(x) is false (a counterexample).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline: produce an x ∈ S that makes P(x) false. Example: show f(11)=121 in the polynomial-prime conjecture to exhibit counterexample. Emphasize that exhibiting how the counterexample makes the statement false (e.g., factoring to show composite) is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproving conditional statements by counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove a conditional ∀x (P(x) ⇒ Q(x)), produce an x for which P(x) is true and Q(x) is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline given: produce x making P true and Q false. This is a specialization of the universal-counterexample technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexample completeness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting a counterexample, explicitly show how the example violates the original claim (don't merely state an example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text warns that simply naming a candidate counterexample without demonstrating the failure (e.g., showing a factorization to prove non-primality) is incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproving existence statements (negation is universal)
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove an existence statement ∃x ∈ S, P(x), prove the universal negation ∀x ∈ S, ¬P(x) instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since the negation is universal, one must produce a proof (direct, contrapositive, or contradiction) that no x satisfies P(x). Example: show ∄ real x with x^4 < x < x^2 by proving for all real x it's false (proof by contradiction shown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproof by contradiction (outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove P by contradiction: assume P is true, derive a contradiction, thereby concluding P is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline: assume P and deduce a logical impossibility. Example: assume ∃x with x^4 < x < x^2, deduce impossible inequality x^2 + x + 1 < 0 for positive x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tables and computational evidence before attempting proof/disproof
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather values or small-case computations to build intuition about a conjecture before attempting proof or disproof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: compute f(n)=n^2 - n + 11 for several n to see pattern; this helps locate counterexample n=11. Tables are recommended as exploratory tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for proof by mathematical induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a sequence of statements S1,S2,... all true: (1) prove the base case S1 (basis step); (2) prove the inductive step that Sk ⇒ S_{k+1} for arbitrary k; conclude all S_n hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domino analogy given. Inductive hypothesis is assuming Sk to prove Sk+1. Basis index may start at 1, 0, or another integer depending on the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of the inductive step and use of the inductive hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: In the inductive step assume S_k is true (the inductive hypothesis) and use it (usually via direct proof) to deduce S_{k+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sum of first n odd numbers, factorial sum identity, Bernoulli's inequality. Show algebraic manipulations that add the (k+1)-th term to the assumed equality/inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility and caveats in choosing base cases for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The base case need not be S1 — it can be S0 or S_m as appropriate. When proving statements over Z (not N), induction must cover backward direction too (e.g., also prove Sk ⇒ S_{k-1} or provide multiple base cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text warns that standard forward induction alone proves statements for n greater than the base; to cover all integers you may need additional steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for proof by strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong induction: prove base case(s) then, for arbitrary k, assume S1 ∧ S2 ∧ ... ∧ S_k and deduce S_{k+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strong induction when Sk ⇒ S_{k+1} is hard but S_m ... S_k together imply S_{k+1}. The domino metaphor is extended: first k dominoes falling make the (k+1)-th fall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tricks and inequality handling in inductive proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with inequalities in induction, you may add unequal quantities to both sides provided the larger side gets the larger addition; you can also drop positive terms to make an inequality weaker when convenient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: adding unequal quantities to preserve inequality direction; removing a positive kx^2 term to simplify to desired inequality in Bernoulli-style induction proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorization of mathematical statements (theorem, conjecture, false)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical statements are categorized as known true (theorems/propositions/lemmas), known false (false statements), or truth unknown (conjectures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the status helps decide whether to attempt a proof or a disproof. Conjectures frequently motivate research; textbook-level conjectures typically are simple to decide with elementary methods.
